studyMetadata.title: Introducing Ecclesiastes
studyMetadata.subtitle: Eight sessions for first-time readers
studyMetadata.description: Ecclesiastes can seem like the strangest book in the Bible. This eight-session study takes first-time readers through eight representative passages, with short summaries of what lies between them, and shows in each session how the book connects to Christ and the New Testament. It works for small groups and for individuals.
studyMetadata.author: Rick Creighton

elements.text:
Ecclesiastes is the Bible’s most surprising book. It is honest about tiredness, injustice and death, and it never rushes to cheer you up. Over eight sessions we shall read eight representative passages, with a short summary of what lies between them, so that by the end you will have a feel for the whole book.

Each session has the same pattern: an opening question, questions on the passage, a short section on how the passage connects to Christ and the New Testament, and three reflection questions. In a group, work through the passage questions together and keep the reflection questions for sharing. On your own, write something for every question; when you have written an answer, tap Check [[icon:localValidate]] to see how it compares.

Tap the Bible reference on a question to read the passage.

If you are leading a group, there are Leaders’ Notes for every session. To switch them on, go to Settings → App → Optional Pages → Leaders’ Notes (this needs Intermediate interface mode).

elements.question: When someone says ‘What’s the point?’ about their work or about life in general, what do you think is usually lying behind the question?

elements.text: Meet the Teacher

elements.passageText:
1The words of the Teacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem: 2“Futile! Futile!” laments the Teacher. “Absolutely futile! Everything is futile!”

3What benefit do people get from all the effort which they expend on earth? 4A generation comes and a generation goes, but the earth remains the same through the ages. 5The sun rises and the sun sets; it hurries away to a place from which it rises again. 6The wind goes to the south and circles around to the north; round and round the wind goes and on its rounds it returns. 7All the streams flow into the sea, but the sea is not full, and to the place where the streams flow, there they will flow again. 8All this monotony is tiresome; no one can bear to describe it. The eye is never satisfied with seeing, nor is the ear ever content with hearing.

9What exists now is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done; there is nothing truly new on earth. 10Is there anything about which someone can say, “Look at this! It is new”? It was already done long ago, before our time. 11No one remembers the former events, nor will anyone remember the events that are yet to happen; they will not be remembered by the future generations.

elements.question: Verses 1–2 speak about the Teacher (‘laments the Teacher’) rather than as the Teacher. What does that suggest about how the book is put together?
elements.questionHint: Notice who is being described, and who is doing the describing.
elements.sampleAnswer: The Teacher is introduced in the third person, so someone other than the Teacher is presenting him and reporting his words. That suggests there are two voices in the book: the Teacher himself, and a narrator who introduces him to us. Later we shall see whether that second voice returns. For now, we are being told to listen to the Teacher while remembering that we are hearing him through someone else.
elements.mainPoint: The book has **two voices**: a narrator who introduces the Teacher, and the Teacher himself, whose words we are about to hear.

elements.question: Verse 2 is the verdict that the rest of the book will test. How is it worded, and what shows how sweeping it is?
elements.questionHint: Look at the repetition and at the last word of the verse.
elements.sampleAnswer: The verdict is that everything is futile, and it is said with heavy repetition: ‘Futile! Futile!’, then ‘Absolutely futile! Everything is futile!’. The word ‘absolutely’ and the word ‘everything’ leave no obvious exceptions. It is a bold claim, and the reader is invited to see whether the Teacher can sustain it.
elements.mainPoint: The Teacher opens with a **sweeping verdict**: everything is futile. The rest of the book tests whether he can sustain it.

elements.text: The question and the evidence

elements.question: What question does the Teacher ask in verse 3, and what evidence do verses 4–7 offer?
elements.questionHint: Look at what stays the same and what keeps moving.
elements.sampleAnswer: He asks what benefit people get from all the effort they expend on earth. The evidence is taken from nature: generations come and go while the earth remains, the sun rises and sets, the wind circles round, and the streams flow into a sea that is never full. Everything moves, but nothing arrives anywhere new.
elements.mainPoint: The Teacher is asking about **lasting benefit**, and nature’s endless cycles are his first evidence that human effort gains little that lasts.

elements.question: What do verses 8–10 add to the picture, and what would the Teacher say to someone proud of a brand-new invention?
elements.questionHint: Think about the eye, the ear, and the word ‘new’.
elements.sampleAnswer: The Teacher says that all this repetition is tiresome and beyond description, and that the eye and ear are never satisfied. He adds that nothing is truly new: what exists now is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done. To the proud inventor he would reply that the thing they call new has probably already been done long ago, before our time.
keyTerms: nothing is truly new|truly new|nothing new
elements.mainPoint: Repetition, weariness and the lack of anything truly new leave **the eye and ear unsatisfied**.

elements.question: Verse 11 says that no one remembers the former events. Why does the Teacher treat being forgotten as part of the problem?
elements.questionHint: Connect verse 11 back to the question of ‘benefit’ in verse 3.
elements.sampleAnswer: If every generation is forgotten by the next, then nothing anyone achieves can leave a lasting mark. That is exactly what the question in verse 3 is probing: whether human effort produces a benefit that lasts. Being forgotten means the effort seems to disappear into the same cycle as everything else.
elements.mainPoint: If everyone is forgotten, **nothing we do can leave a lasting mark**, and that is part of what troubles the Teacher.

elements.question: Verse 2 piles up the word ‘futile’. Judging from verses 3–11, is the Teacher saying that life is worthless, or is something more specific bothering him?
elements.questionHint: Ask what exactly is missing in each of his examples.
elements.sampleAnswer: The examples are all about lasting gain: effort that repeats without getting anywhere, an eye and ear that are never filled, nothing new, and no memory of what came before. He does not say here that life has no value at all; his complaint is that human effort does not secure anything that endures. We shall need to keep watching whether he sticks to that more specific complaint as the book goes on.
elements.mainPoint: The Teacher’s complaint is not that life has no value, but that **human effort secures nothing that lasts**.

elements.text: Looking to Christ

Ecclesiastes is never quoted directly in the New Testament, but one passage in Romans uses the same Greek word that the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament uses for the Teacher’s ‘futile’. Read it and notice what Paul adds.

elements.passageText: 18For I consider that our present sufferings cannot even be compared to the coming glory that will be revealed to us. 19For the creation eagerly waits for the revelation of the sons of God. 20For the creation was subjected to futility—not willingly but because of God who subjected it—in hope 21that the creation itself will also be set free from the bondage of decay into the glorious freedom of God’s children. 22For we know that the whole creation groans and suffers together until now. 23Not only this, but we ourselves also, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we eagerly await our adoption, the redemption of our bodies. 24For in hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope, because who hopes for what he sees? 25But if we hope for what we do not see, we eagerly wait for it with endurance.

elements.question: According to Romans 8:20–21, what was the creation subjected to, who subjected it, and in what hope?
elements.questionHint: Read verses 20 and 21 as one sentence.
elements.sampleAnswer: The creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of God who subjected it. He did this in hope that the creation itself would be set free from the bondage of decay into the glorious freedom of God’s children. So the futility is real, but it is neither the last word nor outside God’s control.
elements.mainPoint: God subjected creation to futility, and **he did it in hope** of its freedom.

elements.question: What does Paul say believers do while they wait (verses 23–25), and how does this differ from the Teacher’s tired ‘nothing truly new’ in Ecclesiastes 1:9?
elements.questionHint: Look for the words ‘groan’, ‘hope’ and ‘eagerly’.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says we groan inwardly, eagerly awaiting our adoption, the redemption of our bodies, having the firstfruits of the Spirit now. We were saved in hope, and we wait for what we cannot yet see with endurance. Where the Teacher sees only repetition, Paul speaks of something genuinely new that is coming, and which has already begun.
elements.mainPoint: Where the Teacher sees only repetition, Paul speaks of **something new that has begun and is still coming**, and we wait for it in hope.

elements.text: Reflect

elements.question: Where in your own life do you feel the ‘round and round’ of Ecclesiastes 1: routine work, chores, the news, the seasons? How do you usually react?
Is there something you have worked hard for that you fear will be forgotten or undone? What does it feel like to say so?
As you begin this study, what do you hope Ecclesiastes will give you, and what do you fear it might do?

elements.text:
Next time we watch the Teacher put his question to the test: he tries pleasure, wealth and achievement to see whether any of them can supply the lasting benefit he is looking for.

A note on words: where the NET says ‘on earth’, many other translations say ‘under the sun’. The phrase draws attention to what can be seen and measured in this life, so keep an eye out for it as we go.
In this session the Teacher stops describing the world and starts experimenting. He is going to try everything a person might hope would make life worthwhile, and report honestly on the result.

What we skipped. In 1:12–18 the Teacher steps forward to speak for himself: ‘I, the Teacher, have been king over Israel in Jerusalem.’ He sets out to examine carefully and thoroughly everything that is done on earth, and calls it a burdensome task that God has given people to keep them occupied. He reports that he became very wise, but that more wisdom only brought more frustration, and he sums it all up as ‘like chasing the wind’.

elements.body: Read Ecclesiastes 1:12–18 before you begin. It takes two minutes and shows the Teacher stepping forward to speak in his own voice.

elements.question: If you could do or have anything you wanted for a year, with no limits on money or time, what would you choose, and do you think it would satisfy you?

elements.text: The experiments

elements.passageText:
1I thought to myself, “Come now, I will try self-indulgent pleasure to see if it is worthwhile.” But I found that it also is futile. 2I said of partying, “It is folly,” and of self-indulgent pleasure, “It accomplishes nothing!” 3I thought deeply about the effects of indulging myself with wine (all the while my mind was guiding me with wisdom) and the effects of behaving foolishly, so that I might discover what is profitable for people to do on earth during the few days of their lives.

4I increased my possessions: I built houses for myself; I planted vineyards for myself. 5I designed royal gardens and parks for myself, and I planted all kinds of fruit trees in them. 6I constructed pools of water for myself, to irrigate my grove of flourishing trees. 7I purchased male and female slaves, and I owned slaves who were born in my house; I also possessed more livestock—both herds and flocks— than any of my predecessors in Jerusalem. 8I also amassed silver and gold for myself, as well as valuable treasures taken from kingdoms and provinces. I acquired male singers and female singers for myself, and what gives a man sensual delight —a harem of beautiful concubines.

9So I was far wealthier than all my predecessors in Jerusalem, yet I maintained my objectivity. 10I did not restrain myself from getting whatever I wanted; I did not deny myself anything that would bring me pleasure. So all my accomplishments gave me joy; this was my reward for all my effort. 11Yet when I reflected on everything I had accomplished and on all the effort that I had expended to accomplish it, I concluded: “All these achievements and possessions are ultimately profitless — like chasing the wind! There is nothing gained from them on earth.”

elements.question: List the things the Teacher tries in verses 1–10. What is striking about the way he goes about it?
elements.questionHint: Look at verse 3 and verses 9–10 as well as the list itself.
elements.sampleAnswer: He tries wine and partying, then building houses, vineyards, gardens and pools, buying slaves and livestock, amassing silver and gold, and acquiring singers and a harem. He does this deliberately, with his mind guiding him with wisdom and keeping his objectivity. He also holds nothing back: he does not deny himself anything that would bring him pleasure.
elements.mainPoint: The Teacher tested pleasure and achievement **thoroughly and deliberately**, holding nothing back.

elements.question: In verse 10 the Teacher says his accomplishments gave him joy; in verse 11 he calls them ‘ultimately profitless’. How can both be true?
elements.questionHint: Notice that verse 11 begins with him stepping back to reflect.
elements.sampleAnswer: The work really did give him joy at the time, and he calls that his reward for the effort. But when he stood back and asked what lasting gain was left, he found nothing that remained. So the joy was real but it could not deliver what he was looking for, which was a benefit that lasts.
elements.mainPoint: The joy was real, but it **could not deliver a lasting gain**.

elements.text: Wisdom and what comes after

elements.passageText:
12Next, I decided to consider wisdom, as well as foolish behavior and ideas. For what more can the king’s successor do than what the king has already done? 13I realized that wisdom is preferable to folly, just as light is preferable to darkness: 14The wise man can see where he is going, but the fool walks in darkness. Yet I also realized that the same fate happens to them both. 15So I thought to myself, “The fate of the fool will happen even to me! Then what did I gain by becoming so excessively wise?” So I lamented to myself, “The benefits of wisdom are ultimately meaningless!” 16For the wise man, like the fool, will not be remembered for very long, because in the days to come, both will already have been forgotten. Alas, the wise man dies—just like the fool! 17So I loathed life because what happens on earth seems awful to me; for all the benefits of wisdom are futile—like chasing the wind.

18So I loathed all the fruit of my effort, for which I worked so hard on earth, because I must leave it behind in the hands of my successor. 19Who knows if he will be a wise man or a fool? Yet he will be master over all the fruit of my labor for which I worked so wisely on earth. This also is futile! 20So I began to despair about all the fruit of my labor for which I worked so hard on earth. 21For a man may do his work with wisdom, knowledge, and skill; however, he must hand over the fruit of his labor as an inheritance to someone else who did not work for it. This also is futile, and an awful injustice! 22What does a man acquire from all his labor and from the anxiety that accompanies his toil on earth? 23For all day long his work produces pain and frustration, and even at night his mind cannot relax. This also is futile!

elements.question: In verses 12–16 the Teacher compares wisdom and folly. What advantage does he give to wisdom, and what is the problem?
elements.questionHint: Look for the pictures of light and darkness, and then for the word ‘yet’.
elements.sampleAnswer: Wisdom is better than folly, as light is better than darkness: the wise person can see where he is going while the fool walks in darkness. The problem is that the same fate happens to both. The wise man dies just like the fool, and both will be forgotten before long, so the Teacher asks what he gained by being so wise.
elements.mainPoint: Wisdom is better than folly, but **death comes to both**, and both are forgotten.

elements.question: Verses 18–23 turn to the fruit of his work. Why does he come to loathe it, and what does he call an ‘awful injustice’?
elements.questionHint: Ask who ends up with what he has built.
elements.sampleAnswer: He must leave everything he has worked for to a successor, and he cannot know whether that person will be wise or foolish. A person may work with wisdom, knowledge and skill, yet hand the fruit to someone who did not work for it, and that is the injustice. Meanwhile the work itself brings pain, anxiety and sleepless nights.
keyTerms: wise or foolish|wise man or a fool|who knows
elements.mainPoint: The sharpest pain of work is **leaving its fruit to someone else**, who may be wise or foolish.

elements.text: The one thing he can recommend

elements.passageText: 24There is nothing better for people than to eat and drink, and to find enjoyment in their work. I also perceived that this ability to find enjoyment comes from God. 25For no one can eat and drink or experience joy apart from him. 26For to the one who pleases him, God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy, but to the sinner, he gives the task of amassing wealth — only to give it to the one who pleases God. This task of the wicked is futile—like chasing the wind!

elements.question: What does the Teacher say in verses 24–25 is ‘better’, and where does he say the ability to enjoy it comes from?
elements.questionHint: The answer to the second part is in both verses.
elements.sampleAnswer: He says there is nothing better than to eat and drink and to find enjoyment in one’s work. He adds that this ability to enjoy comes from God, and that no one can eat or experience joy apart from him. Enjoyment is therefore treated as a gift to be received, not a prize to be earned.
elements.mainPoint: Enjoyment is **a gift from God**, not a prize we earn.

elements.question: Verse 26 divides people into two groups. What does God give to each?
elements.questionHint: Compare what is given to the one who pleases God with what is given to the sinner.
elements.sampleAnswer: To the one who pleases God he gives wisdom, knowledge and joy. To the sinner he gives the task of gathering and amassing wealth, only to hand it over to the one who pleases God. The Teacher calls that task of the wicked futile, like chasing the wind. It is a hard verse, and we should notice that it keeps the question of what God gives at the centre.
elements.mainPoint: This is a hard verse, but it keeps one thing in view: **what we have is given by God**.

elements.text: Looking to Christ
The Teacher’s complaint that a person works hard and then leaves it all to someone else has a close echo in a story Jesus tells in Luke. Read it with chapter 2 in mind.

elements.passageText: 13Then someone from the crowd said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” 14But Jesus said to him, “Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator between you two?” 15Then he said to them, “Watch out and guard yourself from all types of greed, because one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.” 16He then told them a parable: “The land of a certain rich man produced an abundant crop, 17so he thought to himself, ‘What should I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?’ 18Then he said, ‘I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build bigger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. 19And I will say to myself, “You have plenty of goods stored up for many years; relax, eat, drink, celebrate!”’ 20But God said to him, ‘You fool! This very night your life will be demanded back from you, but who will get what you have prepared for yourself?’ 21So it is with the one who stores up riches for himself, but is not rich toward God.”

elements.question: What does the rich man in Jesus’ story plan to do with his harvest, and what does God say to him?
elements.questionHint: Look at his plan in verses 17–19 and God’s reply in verse 20.
elements.sampleAnswer: He plans to pull down his barns and build bigger ones to store all his grain and goods, and then to relax, eat, drink and celebrate for many years. God calls him a fool: that very night his life will be demanded back from him, and he is asked who will get what he has prepared. His plans assume a future that was never his to secure.
elements.mainPoint: The rich man planned for years he did not control, and **God calls him a fool**.

elements.question: Jesus ends by saying the man is ‘not rich toward God’. Where does this agree with the Teacher in chapter 2, and what does Jesus add?
elements.questionHint: Compare Luke 12:20 with Ecclesiastes 2:18–21, then think about verse 21.
elements.sampleAnswer: It agrees that storing up wealth cannot secure a person’s life, because death leaves it to someone else, and Jesus says in verse 15 that life does not consist in an abundance of possessions. Jesus adds a positive alternative: to be rich toward God. The Teacher can only advise enjoying what God gives while it lasts, whereas Jesus points to a kind of wealth that the demand of death does not take away.
elements.mainPoint: Jesus agrees that stored wealth cannot secure a life, and adds the alternative: **be rich toward God**.

elements.text: In 2:12–16 the Teacher observes that the wise man dies just like the fool and is soon forgotten. Throughout the Old Testament the wise man is a recurring figure. But just like prophets, priests and kings, these wise men find their fulfilment in a greater Wise Man who was still to come. The New Testament presents Christ as the true wise man, the wisdom of God. Read how Paul describes him.

elements.passageText:
22For Jews demand miraculous signs and Greeks ask for wisdom, 23but we preach about a crucified Christ, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles. 24But to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. 25For the foolishness of God is wiser than human wisdom, and the weakness of God is stronger than human strength.

26Think about the circumstances of your call, brothers and sisters. Not many were wise by human standards, not many were powerful, not many were born to a privileged position. 27But God chose what the world thinks foolish to shame the wise, and God chose what the world thinks weak to shame the strong. 28God chose what is low and despised in the world, what is regarded as nothing, to set aside what is regarded as something, 29so that no one can boast in his presence. 30He is the reason you have a relationship with Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption, 31so that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”

elements.question: What does Paul say Christ is in 1 Corinthians 1:24, and what does verse 30 say he has become for us? How does this speak to the Teacher’s problem in Ecclesiastes 2:14–16, that the wise man dies like the fool?
elements.questionHint: Look at the list that follows ‘wisdom from God’ in verse 30.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, and that he became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption. The Teacher’s problem is that wisdom cannot rescue even the wise from the same fate as the fool, and both are soon forgotten. Paul says the wisdom we need is a person, who brings righteousness and redemption, which are exactly what folly and death threaten. So the wise man of Ecclesiastes can be read as pointing beyond himself to the one who is the wisdom of God.
keyTerms: power of god|wisdom of god|wisdom from god
elements.mainPoint: The wisdom the Teacher could not find is **a person**: Christ is the wisdom from God.

elements.text: Reflect

elements.question: Of the Teacher’s experiments (pleasure, projects, wealth, achievement), which do you find most tempting? What are you hoping it would give you?
Who will inherit what you have worked for, whether money, a home, a business, a ministry or a reputation? How do you feel about that?
Verse 24 says the ability to enjoy good things comes from God. What simple pleasure could you receive this week as a gift rather than something you have earned?

elements.text: Next time we reach the best-known passage in the book, the poem about ‘a time for everything’, and the Teacher’s reflections on what God is doing in time.

This chapter contains the most famous poem in Ecclesiastes. It is often read at weddings and funerals, but its real subject is bigger: the Teacher is asking what it means that God has fixed the times of our lives, and what we can and cannot know about them.

elements.question: Think of a moment when the timing of something in your life was exactly right, and one when it was terrible. What made the difference?

elements.text: A poem about times

elements.passageText:
1For everything there is an appointed time, and an appropriate time for every activity on earth:

2A time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to uproot what was planted;

3a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;

4a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance.

5A time to throw away stones, and a time to gather stones; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;

6a time to search, and a time to give something up as lost; a time to keep, and a time to throw away;

7a time to rip, and a time to sew; a time to keep silent, and a time to speak.

8A time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace.

elements.question: Look at the pairs in verses 2–8. Which strike you as joyful, which as painful, and which could be either? What does the poem as a whole say about life?
elements.questionHint: Sort the pairs before you decide what the poem is saying.
elements.sampleAnswer: Some of the times are joyful (to be born, to heal, to build up, to laugh, to dance, to embrace, to love, a time for peace) and some are painful (to die, to kill, to weep, to mourn, to hate, a time for war). Others, such as keeping or throwing away, or keeping silent or speaking, depend on the circumstances. Taken together the poem says that life is made of appointed times, good and bad, and that there is a fitting moment for each.
elements.mainPoint: Life is made of **appointed times**, joyful and painful, and each has its moment.

elements.text: What God has done, and what we cannot see

elements.passageText:
9What benefit can a worker gain from his toil? 10I have observed the burden that God has given to people to keep them occupied.

11God has made everything fit beautifully in its appropriate time, but he has also placed ignorance in the human heart so that people cannot discover what God has ordained, from the beginning to the end of their lives.

12I have concluded that there is nothing better for people than to be happy and to enjoy themselves as long as they live, 13and also that everyone should eat and drink, and find enjoyment in all his toil, for these things are a gift from God.

14I also know that whatever God does will endure forever; nothing can be added to it, and nothing taken away from it. God has made it this way, so that men will fear him. 15Whatever exists now has already been, and whatever will be has already been; for God will seek to do again what has occurred in the past.

elements.body: The NET renders the second half of verse 11 in a way that differs from many English Bibles, which say that God has set ‘eternity’ in human hearts. Commentators are divided over the Hebrew word. Either way, the verse goes on to say that people cannot discover what God has done from beginning to end.

elements.question: What two things does verse 11 say about God’s work and about our ability to understand it?
elements.questionHint: The verse has a ‘but’ in the middle.
elements.sampleAnswer: It says that God has made everything fit beautifully in its appropriate time. But it also says that people cannot discover what God has ordained from the beginning of their lives to the end. We can see that what God does is good and fitting, but we cannot see the whole plan.
elements.mainPoint: What God does is **good and fitting in its time**, but we cannot see the whole of his plan.

elements.question: What conclusions does the Teacher draw in verses 12–14 about how to live, and what does he say about the nature of God’s work?
elements.questionHint: Verses 12–13 are about us; verse 14 is about God.
elements.sampleAnswer: He concludes that there is nothing better than to be happy and to enjoy oneself while one lives: to eat and drink and find enjoyment in all one’s toil, which is a gift from God. As for God’s work, it endures for ever, and nothing can be added to it or taken away. God has made it this way so that people will fear him.
elements.mainPoint: The right response to a God we cannot fully see is **to enjoy his gifts and to fear him**.

elements.text: Injustice and death

elements.passageText:
16I saw something else on earth: In the place of justice, there was wickedness, and in the place of fairness, there was wickedness. 17I thought to myself, “God will judge both the righteous and the wicked; for there is an appropriate time for every activity, and there is a time of judgment for every deed.”

18I also thought to myself, “It is for the sake of people, so God can clearly show them that they are like animals. 19For the fate of humans and the fate of animals are the same: As one dies, so dies the other; both have the same breath. There is no advantage for humans over animals, for both are fleeting. 20Both go to the same place, both come from the dust, and to dust both return. 21Who really knows if the human spirit ascends upward, and the animal’s spirit descends into the earth?”

22So I perceived there is nothing better than for people to enjoy their work, because that is their reward; for who can show them what the future holds?

elements.question: What injustice does the Teacher see in verse 16, and what does he tell himself in verse 17?
elements.questionHint: Notice where the wickedness is found.
elements.sampleAnswer: He sees wickedness in the very places where justice and fairness should be found. He tells himself that God will judge both the righteous and the wicked, because there is an appropriate time for every activity and a time of judgment for every deed. So the Teacher holds onto the conviction that God will judge, even though he cannot yet see it.
elements.mainPoint: Even where justice fails, the Teacher holds that **God will judge** every deed.

elements.question: In verses 18–21 the Teacher compares humans and animals. What does he say they share, and what question does he leave open?
elements.questionHint: Look for ‘same’ and ‘who really knows’.
elements.sampleAnswer: He says that humans and animals have the same fate: as one dies, so dies the other, they have the same breath, and both return to dust, so humans have no advantage over animals. Both are fleeting. The open question is in verse 21: who really knows whether the human spirit goes up and the animal’s spirit goes down into the earth?
elements.mainPoint: Humans and animals **share the same death**, and the Teacher honestly leaves open what comes after.

elements.question: Verse 22 ends the chapter. Why does the Teacher say people should enjoy their work, and what limit on our knowledge does he mention?
elements.questionHint: Look for the words ‘reward’ and ‘future’.
elements.sampleAnswer: He says people should enjoy their work because that is their reward, what they are actually given. The limit he mentions is that no one can show them what the future holds. So his advice to enjoy the present rests on how little we can know about what comes after.
keyTerms: after they die|what comes after|after death
elements.mainPoint: Because the future is hidden, **enjoying the work we are given** is the reward the Teacher recommends.

elements.text: Looking to Christ

The Teacher says God has fixed the times but that we cannot see the whole of what he is doing, and he is left asking what happens after death. Two New Testament passages speak to these two themes: Paul on the ‘appropriate time’ God chose, and Paul in Athens on the day God has set.

elements.passageText:
4But when the appropriate time had come, God sent out his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, 5to redeem those who were under the law, so that we may be adopted as sons with full rights.

6And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, who calls “Abba! Father!” 7So you are no longer a slave but a son, and if you are a son, then you are also an heir through God.

elements.question: What did God do ‘when the appropriate time had come’, and why (Galatians 4:4–5)?
elements.questionHint: The answer has two parts: what God did, and what it was for.
elements.sampleAnswer: God sent out his Son, born of a woman and born under the law. He did this to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might be adopted as sons with full rights. The time that the Teacher says we cannot fully see is shown to have a centre: the sending of the Son.
keyTerms: born of a woman|under the law
elements.mainPoint: God’s appropriate time came when **he sent his Son** to redeem us and make us his children.

elements.passageText: 30Therefore, although God has overlooked such times of ignorance, he now commands all people everywhere to repent, 31because he has set a day on which he is going to judge the world in righteousness, by a man whom he designated, having provided proof to everyone by raising him from the dead.”

elements.question: In Acts 17:30–31, what has God set, who will carry it out, and what proof has God given? How does this relate to the Teacher’s thought in Ecclesiastes 3:17?
elements.questionHint: Compare Acts 17:31 with the Teacher’s words about a time of judgment.
elements.sampleAnswer: God has set a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness, by a man whom he designated, and he has given proof to everyone by raising that man from the dead. This confirms what the Teacher told himself in 3:17, that God will judge every deed. It also goes further, because the resurrection of that man shows that death is not the end of the story, which is the very point the Teacher says he cannot know.
elements.mainPoint: God has set a day of judgment and **has given proof of it by raising** the man he appointed.

elements.text: Reflect

elements.question: Which ‘time’ from the poem are you in right now: weeping, waiting, building, letting go? How does it feel to say that God has appointed times?
The Teacher says we cannot see the whole of what God is doing. What is something in your life or in the world that you cannot make sense of at the moment? How do you live with that?
The Teacher sees injustice and says God will judge. Is that a comfort or a worry to you, and why?

elements.text: Next time we stay with injustice and look at a very human response to it: the tears of the oppressed, the restlessness of work, the loneliness of a man with no one to work for, and the strength of two people together.

Chapter 4 begins with some of the bleakest verses in the book and ends with some of its most warm. The Teacher moves from the tears of the oppressed, through the restlessness of work, to a picture of what two people can do that one cannot.

elements.question: Think of a time when you felt completely on your own with a problem. What did you need most?

elements.text: Oppression, envy and loneliness

elements.passageText:
1So I again considered all the oppression that continually occurs on earth. This is what I saw: The oppressed were in tears, but no one was comforting them; no one delivers them from the power of their oppressors. 2So I considered those who are dead and gone more fortunate than those who are still alive. 3But better than both is the one who has not been born and has not seen the evil things that are done on earth.

4Then I considered all the skillful work that is done: Surely it is nothing more than competition between one person and another. This also is profitless—like chasing the wind. 5The fool folds his hands and does no work, so he has nothing to eat but his own flesh. 6Better is one handful with some rest than two hands full of toil and chasing the wind.

7So I again considered another futile thing on earth: 8A man who is all alone with no companion, he has no children nor siblings; yet there is no end to all his toil, and he is never satisfied with riches. He laments, “For whom am I toiling and depriving myself of pleasure?” This also is futile and a burdensome task!

elements.question: What does the Teacher see in verse 1, and what is the one thing the oppressed are missing? What extreme conclusion does he draw in verses 2–3?
elements.questionHint: Notice how often verse 1 mentions comfort and rescue.
elements.sampleAnswer: He sees oppression on earth: the oppressed are in tears, power is on the side of their oppressors, and no one comforts them or delivers them. He concludes that the dead are more fortunate than the living, and that better than both is the one who has never been born, because that person has not seen the evil things that are done on earth. The Teacher is reporting how bleak it looks to him, not recommending despair.
keyTerms: fortunate|dead are better|not been born|never been born
elements.mainPoint: The Teacher **sees oppression with no one to comfort** the oppressed, and his reaction shows how heavy it is.

elements.question: Verse 4 gives one reason people work hard and verse 5 gives the opposite extreme. What do they show, and what does verse 6 recommend?
elements.questionHint: Look for the words ‘competition’ and ‘handful’.
elements.sampleAnswer: Verse 4 says that skilful work is driven by competition between one person and another. Verse 5 shows the opposite extreme: the fool who folds his hands and does no work, and so has nothing to eat but his own flesh. Verse 6 recommends a middle path: better is one handful with some rest than two hands full of toil and chasing the wind.
elements.mainPoint: Work can be driven by **envy** or ruined by idleness; better is a handful held with quiet.

elements.question: Describe the man in verses 7–8. What question does he ask himself, and why is it so painful?
elements.questionHint: Look at what he does not have as well as what he has.
elements.sampleAnswer: He is completely alone, with no companion, no children and no siblings, yet there is no end to his toil and he is never satisfied with riches. He asks ‘For whom am I toiling?’, and the pain is that he has no one to share the fruit with and no purpose beyond himself. The Teacher calls it futile and a burdensome task.
elements.mainPoint: Endless toil with **no one to share it** is futile and painful.

elements.text: Two are better than one

elements.passageText: 9Two people are better than one, because they can reap more benefit from their labor. 10For if they fall, one will help his companion up, but pity the person who falls down and has no one to help him up. 11Furthermore, if two lie down together, they can keep each other warm, but how can one person keep warm by himself? 12Although an assailant may overpower one person, two can withstand him. Moreover, a three-stranded cord is not quickly broken.

elements.question: What reasons does the Teacher give in verses 9–12 for why two are better than one?
elements.questionHint: There are several; read each verse for a separate picture.
elements.sampleAnswer: Two can reap more benefit from their labour. If one falls the other can help him up, while the person who falls alone has no one. Two lying together keep each other warm, and two can withstand an attacker who would overpower one. The three-stranded cord that is not quickly broken sums up the point.
elements.mainPoint: Two are better than one: **shared work, help, warmth and defence**.

elements.question: How do verses 9–12 answer the question of the lonely man in verse 8?
elements.questionHint: Start from his question, ‘For whom?’
elements.sampleAnswer: His problem was having no one to work for and no one to share the result with. Verses 9–12 show that with a companion, work brings a better return and the rewards are shared, and troubles are shared too. The work is no longer a closed circle ending in himself, and so it has a point.
keyTerms: for whom|no one to work for|alone
elements.mainPoint: Companionship gives work **a purpose beyond ourselves**.

elements.question: Compare verse 1 with verse 10. What does the oppressed person of verse 1 lack that verse 10 says a companion provides?
elements.questionHint: Think about the word ‘comfort’ and the words ‘help him up’.
elements.sampleAnswer: In verse 1 the oppressed are in tears with no one to comfort or deliver them. In verse 10 the person who falls can be helped up by a companion, while the person who falls alone is to be pitied. What is missing in both is another person who will stand with the one who is down. The Teacher does not claim this removes oppression, but it shows how much it matters not to be alone.
elements.mainPoint: The oppressed and the fallen alike need **someone to stand with them**.

elements.text: Looking to Christ

Ecclesiastes 4 shows the oppressed with no one to help them, and the value of a companion for the one who falls. Two New Testament passages take up these themes: Jesus announcing his mission to the oppressed in Nazareth, and Paul describing how Christians are to carry one another.

elements.passageText: 16Now Jesus came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day, as was his custom. He stood up to read, 17and the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written, 18“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim release to the captives and the regaining of sight to the blind, to set free those who are oppressed, 19to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.” 20Then he rolled up the scroll, gave it back to the attendant, and sat down. The eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed on him. 21Then he began to tell them, “Today this scripture has been fulfilled even as you heard it being read.”

elements.question: What does Jesus read from Isaiah in Luke 4:18–19, and what does he say about it in verse 21?
elements.questionHint: Look at who the good news is for.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus reads that the Spirit of the Lord is upon him and has anointed him to proclaim good news to the poor, release to the captives, sight to the blind, and to set free those who are oppressed. He then says that today this scripture has been fulfilled in the hearing of his listeners. Where the Teacher saw the oppressed with no one to deliver them, Jesus announces that he has come to do exactly that.
elements.mainPoint: Jesus announces **good news and freedom for the oppressed**, and says it is fulfilled today.

elements.passageText: 1Brothers and sisters, if a person is discovered in some sin, you who are spiritual restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness. Pay close attention to yourselves, so that you are not tempted too. 2Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.

elements.question: What does Paul tell Christians to do for one another in Galatians 6:1–2, and how does this compare with the picture that two people are better than one?
elements.questionHint: Notice the words ‘gentleness’, ‘burdens’ and ‘law of Christ’.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says that those who are spiritual should restore a person caught in sin in a spirit of gentleness, while watching themselves, and that we should carry one another’s burdens and so fulfil the law of Christ. Like the Teacher, Paul sees that people need someone to help them up when they fall. But he grounds the help in Christ, and the help includes gentle restoration of those who have failed.
elements.mainPoint: Christians are to **carry one another’s burdens** and gently restore those who fall.

elements.text: Reflect

elements.question: Who is carrying you at the moment, and who might you carry? What stops you from asking for help or offering it?
The Teacher sees the tears of the oppressed and no one to comfort them. Where do you see that today, in your community or in the news? What could you do about it, however small?
Which is closer to your life at present: working out of competition and envy, or working with quiet? What would ‘one handful with some rest’ look like for you this week?

elements.text: Next time we skip the story of the poor wise youth and the old foolish king (4:13–16), and go straight to the temple, where the Teacher gives advice about how to speak to God.

This is the passage in Ecclesiastes that is most directly about worship at the temple. After chapters of observation, the Teacher turns to practical advice: how should a person speak to God, and what should they promise him?

What we skipped. In 4:13–16 the Teacher tells a short story about a poor but wise youth who rises to replace an old and foolish king, and observes that even the popularity of a ruler like that fades with the next generation. It is another example of how little lasting benefit comes from status and power.

elements.body: Read Ecclesiastes 4:13–16 before you begin. It is only four verses, and it is a good example of the Teacher’s short ‘anecdotes’.

elements.question: When you go to a place of worship, or settle down to pray, what do you usually expect to do: speak, listen, sing, or something else?

elements.text: Going to God’s house

elements.passageText:
1Be careful what you do when you go to the temple of God; draw near to listen rather than to offer a sacrifice like fools, for they do not realize that they are doing wrong.

2Do not be rash with your mouth or hasty in your heart to bring up a matter before God, for God is in heaven and you are on earth! Therefore, let your words be few. 3Just as dreams come when there are many cares, so the rash vow of a fool occurs when there are many words.

4When you make a vow to God, do not delay in paying it. For God takes no pleasure in fools: Pay what you vow! 5It is better for you not to vow than to vow and not pay it.

6Do not let your mouth cause you to sin, and do not tell the priest, “It was a mistake!” Why make God angry at you so that he would destroy the work of your hands? 7Just as there is futility in many dreams, so also in many words. Therefore, fear God.

elements.question: What does verse 1 tell us to do on entering God’s house, and what comparison is made with fools?
elements.questionHint: Look for the contrast between listening and offering.
elements.sampleAnswer: We are to be careful what we do and to draw near to listen rather than to offer a sacrifice as fools do. The fools do not realise that they are doing wrong. So the advice is that listening to God comes before offering anything to him, and that hasty worship can be wrong without the worshipper knowing.
elements.mainPoint: Approach God by **listening first**, not by rushing to offer something.

elements.question: Verse 2 gives a reason for letting our words be few. What is it?
elements.questionHint: The reason is in the last sentence of the verse.
elements.sampleAnswer: The reason is that God is in heaven and we are on earth. Because of that distance we should not be rash with our mouths or hasty in our hearts to bring up a matter before God. Therefore, the verse says, let our words be few.
elements.mainPoint: Because God is in heaven and we are on earth, **our words should be few**.

elements.question: What two comparisons with dreams does the passage make, in verses 3 and 7?
elements.questionHint: Read verse 3 and verse 7 side by side.
elements.sampleAnswer: Verse 3 says that just as dreams come when there are many cares, so the rash vow of a fool occurs when there are many words. Verse 7 says that just as there is futility in many dreams, so also in many words. In both, many words are compared with dreams: they are insubstantial, and they tend to run ahead of what the speaker can deliver.
elements.mainPoint: Many words, like many dreams, are **insubstantial**.

elements.question: What does the passage say about making vows in verses 4–5?
elements.questionHint: There are three short instructions.
elements.sampleAnswer: A vow made to God must not be delayed in the paying, because God takes no pleasure in fools. The passage says plainly to pay what is vowed. It adds that it is better not to vow at all than to vow and not pay.
keyTerms: better not to vow|not to vow
elements.mainPoint: Vows must be **kept**, and it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay.

elements.question: What consequences does verse 6 give for rash words and excuses?
elements.questionHint: Notice what the mouth can do, and what God can do.
elements.sampleAnswer: The mouth can cause a person to sin. Telling the priest that the vow was a mistake does not solve it. The verse asks why a person would make God angry at them, so that he destroys the work of their hands.
keyTerms: angry|destroy|work of your hands|work of their hands
elements.mainPoint: Careless words can have real consequences, because **God takes them seriously**.

elements.question: Verse 7 ends with a short command. Why does ‘Therefore, fear God’ fit as the conclusion of the whole passage?
elements.questionHint: Think how each earlier instruction expresses taking God seriously.
elements.sampleAnswer: Each earlier instruction is a way of taking God seriously as God: listening before speaking, keeping our words few, and keeping our vows. Fear here means reverent respect before the one who is in heaven while we are on earth. It does not mean silence for its own sake, but taking care that what we say to God matches who he is.
elements.mainPoint: Fearing God means **taking him seriously** in every word we say to him.

elements.text: Looking to Christ

The Teacher says that God is in heaven and we are on earth, so we should come carefully. The letter to the Hebrews says that something has changed about how we come. Jesus also taught his followers not to pile up words when they pray, in Matthew 6:7–8, and to address God as ‘our Father in heaven’ (Matthew 6:9).

elements.passageText: 14Therefore since we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast to our confession. 15For we do not have a high priest incapable of sympathizing with our weaknesses, but one who has been tempted in every way just as we are, yet without sin. 16Therefore let us confidently approach the throne of grace to receive mercy and find grace whenever we need help.

elements.question: Who is the ‘great high priest’ of verse 14, where is he, and how does verse 15 describe him?
elements.questionHint: Look for the name, the place, and the word ‘sympathizing’.
elements.sampleAnswer: He is Jesus the Son of God, who has passed through the heavens. Verse 15 says that he is a high priest who can sympathise with our weaknesses, because he has been tempted in every way just as we are, yet without sin. The one who is in heaven is therefore not distant from our weakness.
elements.mainPoint: Jesus is a great high priest who **has been where we are** and sympathises with our weakness.

elements.question: How does verse 16 invite us to come to God, and how does this keep or change the Teacher’s advice in Ecclesiastes 5:1–2?
elements.questionHint: Notice that the invitation is to a throne.
elements.sampleAnswer: We are invited to approach the throne of grace confidently, to receive mercy and find grace whenever we need help. The seriousness the Teacher asks for remains, because it is still a throne. What changes is that, because of Jesus, the way in is open and we can come with confidence instead of fear of getting it wrong.
elements.mainPoint: Because of Jesus we may **come to the throne of grace with confidence**, and still with reverence.

elements.text: Reflect

elements.question: How easy do you find it to ‘draw near to listen’ rather than to do or say something? What gets in the way?
Is there a promise you have made, to God or to someone else, that you have not yet kept? What would it look like to deal with it honestly?
Hebrews invites us to approach with confidence, and Ecclesiastes asks for care and few words. How could you hold both when you pray this week?

elements.text: Next time we turn to money. The Teacher asks what it can and cannot do for the people who pursue it, and what it means to receive wealth as a gift.

chapters.chapterTitle: Money and the gift of God

elements.text: Money is one of the Teacher’s steadiest themes. This passage shows what the love of money does to a person, and sets alongside it a very different picture: wealth received as a gift that can be enjoyed.

What we skipped. In 5:8–9 the Teacher says that when you see the poor being squeezed and justice perverted in government, you should not be astonished: officials are watched by higher officials, and everyone, even the king, depends on the produce of the land. It is a sober remark about how widespread the problem is.

elements.body: Read Ecclesiastes 5:8–9 before you begin. It is two verses, and it sets the scene for what follows about money.

elements.question: What would ‘enough’ look like for you: enough money, enough possessions, enough recognition?

elements.text: The love of money

elements.passageText:
10The one who loves money will never be satisfied with money, he who loves wealth will never be satisfied with his income. This also is futile. 11When someone’s prosperity increases, those who consume it also increase; so what does its owner gain, except that he gets to see it with his eyes? 12The sleep of the laborer is pleasant—whether he eats little or much— but the wealth of the rich will not allow him to sleep.

13Here is a misfortune on earth that I have seen: Wealth hoarded by its owner to his own misery. 14Then that wealth was lost through bad luck; although he fathered a son, he has nothing left to give him. 15Just as he came forth from his mother’s womb, naked will he return as he came, and he will take nothing in his hand that he may carry away from his toil. 16This is another misfortune: Just as he came, so will he go. What did he gain from toiling for the wind? 17Surely, he ate in darkness every day of his life, and he suffered greatly with sickness and anger.

elements.question: What three observations about wealth does the Teacher make in verses 10–12?
elements.questionHint: One is about desire, one about who benefits, and one about sleep.
elements.sampleAnswer: The first is that the one who loves money is never satisfied with it. The second is that when prosperity increases, so do those who consume it, so the owner gains little beyond seeing it with his eyes. The third is that the labourer sleeps well, whether he eats little or much, while the abundance of the rich does not let them sleep.
elements.mainPoint: Wealth does not satisfy: **those who love money always want more**, and it can cost them their sleep.

elements.question: Why might the labourer sleep better than the rich man in verse 12?
elements.questionHint: Think about what the rich man has to worry about.
elements.sampleAnswer: The labourer’s sleep is pleasant whatever he has to eat, which suggests that he is content with what he has and has nothing to guard. The rich person’s wealth will not allow him to sleep, which suggests anxiety about protecting and increasing it. The difference lies in the burden of the wealth, not the amount of it.
elements.mainPoint: **Contentment**, not abundance, brings rest.

elements.question: Tell the story of the rich man in verses 13–14. What goes wrong?
elements.questionHint: Look for what he did with his wealth and what happened to it.
elements.sampleAnswer: He hoarded his wealth, to his own misery. Then the wealth was lost through some misfortune. Although he had a son, he had nothing left to give him.
elements.mainPoint: Hoarded wealth can end in **loss**, with nothing left to pass on.

elements.question: Verses 15–17 follow the man to the end of his life. What do they say, and how is his life described in verse 17?
elements.questionHint: Look at what he brings and what he takes.
elements.sampleAnswer: He came naked from his mother’s womb and will go the same way, taking nothing in his hand from his toil. The Teacher asks what he gained from toiling for the wind. Verse 17 says that he ate in darkness all his days, and suffered greatly with sickness and anger.
elements.mainPoint: We leave life as we entered it, and **a life spent grasping ends in darkness**.

elements.text: The gift of God

elements.passageText: 18I have seen personally what is the only beneficial and appropriate course of action for people: to eat and drink, and find enjoyment in all their hard work on earth during the few days of their life that God has given them, for this is their reward. 19To every man whom God has given wealth and possessions, he has also given him the ability to eat from them, to receive his reward, and to find enjoyment in his toil; these things are the gift of God. 20For he does not think much about the fleeting days of his life because God keeps him preoccupied with the joy he derives from his activity.

elements.question: What does the Teacher say in verses 18–19 is the only beneficial and appropriate course of action, and what does he say God gives?
elements.questionHint: Look for the words ‘gift’ and ‘ability’.
elements.sampleAnswer: He says it is to eat and drink and find enjoyment in all one’s hard work during the few days of life that God has given, for this is the reward. God gives some people wealth and possessions, and also the ability to eat from them, to receive their reward and to find enjoyment in their toil. These things, he says, are the gift of God.
elements.mainPoint: The best use of wealth is **to enjoy it as a gift from God**.

elements.question: Verse 20 says God keeps such a person preoccupied with the joy of their activity. How is this different from the man in verses 13–17?
elements.questionHint: Compare what occupies each man’s mind.
elements.sampleAnswer: The man in verses 13–17 is consumed by hoarding, loss and bitterness, and he eats in darkness. The person in verse 20 is kept occupied by joy, and does not brood on the fleeting days of life. The difference is not mainly how much each has, but whether what they have is received as a gift from God and enjoyed.
elements.mainPoint: The difference is **not how much we have**, but whether we receive it as God’s gift.

elements.text: Looking to Christ
The New Testament says a good deal about money, and Paul’s advice to Timothy covers both sides of this passage: the danger of the love of money, and the enjoyment of God’s gifts.

elements.passageText: 6Now godliness combined with contentment brings great profit. 7For we have brought nothing into this world and so we cannot take a single thing out either. 8But if we have food and shelter, we will be satisfied with that. 9Those who long to be rich, however, stumble into temptation and a trap and many senseless and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. 10For the love of money is the root of all evils. Some people in reaching for it have strayed from the faith and stabbed themselves with many pains.

elements.question: What does Paul say brings ‘great profit’ in 1 Timothy 6:6, and what is the danger for those who long to be rich (verses 9–10)?
elements.questionHint: Notice the word ‘contentment’ and the word ‘trap’.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says that godliness combined with contentment brings great profit, and that if we have food and shelter we will be satisfied. Those who long to be rich stumble into temptation and a trap and into many senseless and harmful desires that lead to ruin. The love of money is the root of all evils, and some who reach for it have strayed from the faith and stabbed themselves with many pains.
elements.mainPoint: **Godliness with contentment** is the real gain; the love of money destroys.

elements.passageText: 17Command those who are rich in this world’s goods not to be haughty or to set their hope on riches, which are uncertain, but on God who richly provides us with all things for our enjoyment. 18Tell them to do good, to be rich in good deeds, to be generous givers, sharing with others. 19In this way they will save up a treasure for themselves as a firm foundation for the future and so lay hold of what is truly life.

elements.question: In 1 Timothy 6:17–19, where are the rich told to set their hope, what does Paul say about God’s gifts, and what are the rich to do? How does verse 17 compare with Ecclesiastes 5:18–19?
elements.questionHint: Compare 6:17 with the ‘gift of God’ in 5:19.
elements.sampleAnswer: The rich are to set their hope on God and not on uncertain riches, and God is the one who richly provides us with all things for our enjoyment. They are to do good, be rich in good deeds, and be generous givers who share with others. Both passages agree that enjoyment is God’s gift, and Paul adds generosity, and a treasure for the future that lays hold of what is truly life.
elements.mainPoint: Set your hope on God, not riches, and **enjoy and share** what he provides.

elements.text: Reflect

elements.question: Where do you notice wanting more turning into never being satisfied in your own life?
What does it say about where your hope is when you sleep well, or when you do not?
What is a gift from God that you could enjoy and share this week?

elements.text: Next time we move to chapter 9, where the Teacher faces death head on, and asks how a person should live when no one can control the length of their days.

chapters.chapterTitle: Death and the days we have

elements.text: Death has been in the background of every session so far. In chapter 9 the Teacher looks at it directly, and then gives one of the most vivid pieces of advice in the book about how to live in its shadow.

What we skipped. Chapter 6 describes people who have wealth but cannot enjoy it, and asks who knows what is good for a person in their brief life. Chapter 7 is a collection of ‘better than’ sayings and some puzzling advice about not being over-righteous and over-wise, with the observation that no one on earth always does good and never sins. Chapter 8 deals with kings and justice: the Teacher advises obeying authority, but admits that the wicked sometimes seem to prosper and that no one can fully find out what God is doing.

elements.body: If you can, read Ecclesiastes 7:15–29 and 8:10–17 before you begin. They show the Teacher wrestling with the question of why life seems unfair, which lies behind the passage we are about to read.

elements.question: When did you last go to a funeral, or visit a grave? What went through your mind?

elements.text: The same fate for everyone

elements.passageText:
1So I reflected on all this, attempting to clear it all up. I concluded that the righteous and the wise, as well as their works, are in the hand of God; whether a person will be loved or hated — no one knows what lies ahead. 2Everyone shares the same fate — the righteous and the wicked, the good and the bad, the ceremonially clean and unclean, those who offer sacrifices and those who do not. What happens to the good person, also happens to the sinner; what happens to those who make vows, also happens to those who are afraid to make vows. 3This is the unfortunate fact about everything that happens on earth: the same fate awaits everyone. In addition to this, the hearts of all people are full of evil, and there is folly in their hearts during their lives—then they die.

4But whoever is among the living has hope; a live dog is better than a dead lion. 5For the living know that they will die, but the dead do not know anything; they have no further reward—and even the memory of them disappears. 6What they loved, as well as what they hated and envied, perished long ago, and they no longer have a part in anything that happens on earth.

elements.question: According to verses 1–3, what do the righteous and the wicked share, and what do people not know?
elements.questionHint: Look at the list in verse 2 and at the end of verse 1.
elements.sampleAnswer: The righteous and the wicked, the good and the bad, the clean and the unclean, those who offer sacrifices and those who do not, all share the same fate. The righteous and the wise are in the hand of God, yet no one knows whether love or hatred lies ahead. The hearts of all are full of evil and folly, and then they die.
elements.mainPoint: **Death comes to everyone**, righteous or wicked, and we do not know what lies ahead in this life.

elements.question: Verse 4 says that a live dog is better than a dead lion. What reasons for the advantage of the living do verses 4–6 give?
elements.questionHint: Think about what the living know that the dead do not.
elements.sampleAnswer: The living have hope. The living know that they will die, whereas the dead know nothing and have no further reward, and even the memory of them disappears. What they loved, hated and envied has perished, and they no longer have a part in anything that happens on earth.
elements.mainPoint: The living have **hope and a share in life on earth**, which the dead no longer have.

elements.text: Enjoy life while you can

elements.passageText: 7Go, eat your food with joy, and drink your wine with a happy heart, because God has already approved your works. 8Let your clothes always be white, and do not spare precious ointment on your head. 9Enjoy life with your beloved wife during all the days of your fleeting life that God has given you on earth during all your fleeting days; for that is your reward in life and in your burdensome work on earth. 10Whatever you find to do with your hands, do it with all your might, because there is neither work nor planning nor knowledge nor wisdom in the grave, the place where you will eventually go.

elements.question: List the commands in verses 7–10. What kind of life do they describe?
elements.questionHint: There are about six commands.
elements.sampleAnswer: The commands are to eat your food with joy, drink your wine with a happy heart, wear white clothes always, not spare the ointment on your head, enjoy life with your beloved wife, and do whatever you find to do with all your might. The picture is of a festive, joyful, relational and energetic life, in which ordinary pleasures are received gladly and work is done wholeheartedly. Nothing in the list is extravagant; it is the ordinary good things of daily life.
elements.mainPoint: The call is to **enjoy the ordinary good things** of life wholeheartedly.

elements.question: What reasons does the Teacher give for living like this?
elements.questionHint: Look for ‘because’ in verse 7, and for the words ‘reward’ and ‘grave’.
elements.sampleAnswer: In verse 7 he says that God has already approved your works. In verse 9 he says that this is your reward in life and in your burdensome work, and he reminds us that our days are fleeting. In verse 10 he adds that there is neither work nor planning nor knowledge nor wisdom in the grave, the place where you will eventually go.
elements.mainPoint: We can enjoy life because **God has approved it**, because it is our reward, and because it is brief.

elements.text: No one knows the time

elements.passageText: 11Again, I observed this on the earth: the race is not always won by the swiftest, the battle is not always won by the strongest; prosperity does not always belong to those who are the wisest, wealth does not always belong to those who are the most discerning, nor does success always come to those with the most knowledge— for time and chance may overcome them all. 12Surely, no one knows his appointed time. Like fish that are caught in a deadly net, and like birds that are caught in a snare— just like them, all people are ensnared at an unfortunate time that falls upon them suddenly.

elements.question: What examples does the Teacher give in verse 11 of the best not always winning, and what picture does verse 12 use?
elements.questionHint: Count the examples in verse 11.
elements.sampleAnswer: The race is not always won by the swiftest, nor the battle by the strongest, nor prosperity by the wisest, nor wealth by the most discerning, nor success by those with knowledge. Verse 12 says that no one knows their appointed time. Like fish caught in a deadly net and birds caught in a snare, people are caught suddenly at an unfortunate time.
elements.mainPoint: Success is not guaranteed: **time and chance** come to all, and no one knows when.

elements.question: How does the advice to enjoy life in verses 7–10 follow from what he has said about death in verses 1–6 and about chance in verses 11–12?
elements.questionHint: Ask what is left to do once death is certain and its timing is not.
elements.sampleAnswer: If death comes to everyone and no one can predict or control when it comes, then the sensible course is to receive and enjoy the gifts of today while you have them. His advice is made urgent by mortality. His joy is real, but it is a joy under the shadow of death, with nothing said here about hope beyond the grave.
elements.mainPoint: Because death is certain and its timing hidden, **today’s gifts are to be received now**.

elements.text: Looking to Christ
The Teacher says the dead know nothing and that no one can say what lies beyond. The New Testament speaks directly to that. Two passages show what changes when Christ rises from the dead.

elements.passageText: 21Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. 22But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will grant you.” 23Jesus replied, “Your brother will come back to life again.” 24Martha said, “I know that he will come back to life again in the resurrection at the last day.” 25Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in me will live even if he dies, 26and the one who lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?” 27She replied, “Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God who comes into the world.”

elements.question: What does Martha say she knows in verses 22–24, and what does Jesus say about himself in verses 25–26?
elements.questionHint: Compare what Martha believes about the last day with what Jesus says about himself.
elements.sampleAnswer: Martha says that she knows God will grant whatever Jesus asks, and that her brother will rise in the resurrection at the last day. Jesus says that he himself is the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in him will live even if he dies, and the one who lives and believes in him will never die.
elements.mainPoint: Jesus is **the resurrection and the life**: those who believe in him will live even though they die.

elements.passageText: 54Now when this perishable puts on the imperishable, and this mortal puts on immortality, then the saying that is written will happen, “Death has been swallowed up in victory.” 55“Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” 56The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. 57But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ! 58So then, dear brothers and sisters, be firm. Do not be moved! Always be outstanding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.

elements.question: What does Paul say happens to death in 1 Corinthians 15:54–57, and what does he conclude about work in verse 58? How is this different from Ecclesiastes 9:10?
elements.questionHint: Compare ‘no work’ in the grave with ‘not in vain’.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says that death is swallowed up in victory, and that God gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. He concludes that his readers should be firm and always outstanding in the work of the Lord, knowing that their labour is not in vain in the Lord. The Teacher says to work with all your might because there is no work in the grave, whereas Paul says to work because, in Christ, your work is not wasted.
elements.mainPoint: In Christ **death is swallowed up in victory**, so our work is not in vain.

elements.text: Reflect

elements.question: The Teacher says a live dog is better than a dead lion, while Jesus says death is not the end. How does knowing that you will die affect the way you live?
Which of the commands in verses 7–10 is hardest for you to obey, and why?
Is there someone you should share a meal or a good day with before time runs out? What would it take to do it this week?

elements.text: Next time we reach the end of the book: the Teacher’s advice to the young, his picture of old age, and the voice that closes the book and tells us what to make of him.
We end where the book ends. The Teacher speaks to the young about joy and old age, and then another voice speaks about him and gives the conclusion of the whole book.

What we skipped. In 9:13–18 the Teacher tells another short story, about a poor wise man who saved a city and was soon forgotten, and observes that wisdom is better than strength even when it is despised. Chapter 10 is a string of proverbs about folly, rulers and work, showing how a little folly can spoil a great deal of wisdom. In 11:1–6 he urges bold but sensible action in the face of uncertainty: invest generously, and keep sowing, since no one can know in advance which efforts will succeed.

elements.body: If you can, read Ecclesiastes 11:1–6 before you begin. It is the Teacher’s advice for living when the future is hidden, and it leads directly into our passage.

elements.question: How would you finish this sentence: ‘The most important thing I have learned from Ecclesiastes so far is…’?

elements.text: Rejoice, and remember

elements.passageText:
7Light is sweet, and it is pleasant for a person to see the sun. 8So, if a man lives many years, let him rejoice in them all, but let him remember that the days of darkness will be many—all that is about to come is obscure.

9Rejoice, young man, while you are young, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth. Follow the impulses of your heart and the desires of your eyes, but know that God will judge your motives and actions. 10Banish emotional stress from your mind. and put away pain from your body; for youth and the prime of life are fleeting.

12:1So remember your Creator in the days of your youth— before the difficult days come, and the years draw near when you will say, “I have no pleasure in them”; 2before the sun and the light of the moon and the stars grow dark, and the clouds disappear after the rain;

3when those who keep watch over the house begin to tremble, and the virile men begin to stoop over, and the grinders begin to cease because they grow few, and those who look through the windows grow dim, 4and the doors along the street are shut; when the sound of the grinding mill grows low, and one is awakened by the sound of a bird, and all their songs grow faint, 5and they are afraid of heights and the dangers in the street; the almond blossoms grow white, and the grasshopper drags itself along, and the caper berry shrivels up — because man goes to his eternal home, and the mourners go about in the streets—

6before the silver cord is removed, or the golden bowl is broken, or the pitcher is shattered at the well, or the water wheel is broken at the cistern— 7and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the life’s breath returns to God who gave it.

elements.question: What does the Teacher tell the young to do in 11:7–10, and what two things does he want them to keep in mind?
elements.questionHint: Look at verses 8 and 9 for the two reminders.
elements.sampleAnswer: He tells the young to rejoice, to let their hearts cheer them in the days of their youth, and to follow the impulses of their hearts and the desires of their eyes. He wants them to remember that the days of darkness will be many, and to know that God will judge their motives and actions. So the joy he commends is real, and it comes with a reminder of death and of God’s judgment.
elements.mainPoint: Rejoice in youth, **remembering** that dark days and God’s judgment lie ahead.

elements.question: Chapter 12 begins with the command ‘remember your Creator’. What are the pictures in verses 1–5 about?
elements.questionHint: Look at what is said about light, strength, sight and hearing.
elements.sampleAnswer: They are most naturally read as pictures of old age and the approach of death. The light grows dark, those who keep watch tremble, the strong stoop, the grinders cease because they grow few, those who look through windows grow dim, hearing fades, and people fear heights and the dangers in the street. The almond blossom turns white and the grasshopper drags itself along, all because man goes to his eternal home.
elements.mainPoint: The pictures describe **old age and the approach of death**.

elements.question: How does the passage describe death in verses 5–7?
elements.questionHint: Look at what returns to where, and what is said about mourners.
elements.sampleAnswer: A person goes to their eternal home and mourners go about in the streets. The silver cord is removed, the golden bowl is broken, and the pitcher and water wheel are shattered. The dust returns to the earth as it was, while the life’s breath returns to God who gave it.
elements.mainPoint: Death is a return: **dust to the earth, breath to God**.

elements.text: The voice at the end

elements.passageText:
8“Absolutely futile!” laments the Teacher, “All these things are futile!” 9Not only was the Teacher wise, but he also taught knowledge to the people; he carefully evaluated and arranged many proverbs. 10The Teacher sought to find delightful words, and to write accurately truthful sayings. 11The words of the sages are like prods, and the collected sayings are like firmly fixed nails; they are given by one shepherd.

12Be warned, my son, of anything in addition to them. There is no end to the making of many books, and much study is exhausting to the body. 13Having heard everything, I have reached this conclusion: Fear God and keep his commandments, because this is the whole duty of man. 14For God will evaluate every deed, including every secret thing, whether good or evil.
