elements.question: Look at who is speaking in verses 8–11. How does this voice differ from the ‘I’ of earlier chapters, and what does it say about the Teacher?
elements.questionHint: Compare verse 8 with 1:1–2, and with 1:12.
elements.sampleAnswer: Here the Teacher is spoken about in the third person, as ‘the Teacher’, rather than speaking as ‘I’ as he did from 1:12. This is the same kind of voice as the one that introduced him in 1:1–2, so the book has a voice at the beginning and the end that surrounds the Teacher’s own speech. This voice praises the Teacher as wise, as someone who taught knowledge, weighed and arranged many proverbs, and sought delightful words and accurate, truthful sayings.
elements.mainPoint: A second voice speaks **about** the Teacher, and praises his wise words.

elements.question: What picture does verse 11 give of wise sayings, and why might ‘prods’ and ‘firmly fixed nails’ be good images?
elements.questionHint: Think about what each tool does.
elements.sampleAnswer: The words of the sages are compared to prods and to firmly fixed nails, and the collected sayings are said to be given by one shepherd. A prod moves a person or an animal on, and a fixed nail holds something steady. Wise sayings do both: they provoke us to move, and they hold us in place.
elements.mainPoint: Wise sayings **prod us on and hold us steady**.

elements.question: What is the final conclusion in verses 13–14, and what reason is given for it?
elements.questionHint: The reason is in verse 14.
elements.sampleAnswer: The conclusion is to fear God and keep his commandments, because this is the whole duty of man. The reason is that God will evaluate every deed, including every secret thing, whether good or evil. So the book ends not with the refrain but with reverence for God and accountability to him.
elements.mainPoint: The book ends by **fearing God and keeping his commandments**, because he will judge every deed.

elements.text: Looking to Christ

The epilogue praises the Teacher as a wise man whose words prod and steady us, and it ends with God’s judgment of every deed. The New Testament presents Christ as the true wise man, the wisdom of God. It also speaks of a shepherd, and of judgment. Readers have understood ‘one shepherd’ in 12:11 in different ways, so we shall not decide that here. Three passages follow.

elements.passageText: 1For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you, and for those in Laodicea, and for those who have not met me face to face. 2My goal is that their hearts, having been knit together in love, may be encouraged, and that they may have all the riches that assurance brings in their understanding of the knowledge of the mystery of God, namely, Christ, 3in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

elements.question: What does Paul want for his readers in Colossians 2:2, and what does he say is hidden in Christ (verse 3)? How does this bring the Teacher’s search for wisdom to a point?
elements.questionHint: Compare verse 3 with the Teacher’s weighing and arranging of proverbs in 12:9.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul wants their hearts to be encouraged and knit together in love, with all the riches that assurance brings in understanding the mystery of God, namely Christ. He says that in Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. The Teacher spent his life searching and weighing proverbs, and found that no one can discover everything God has done. Paul says the wisdom is found in a person, so the wise man of Ecclesiastes can be seen as a pointer to Christ, in whom the wisdom the Teacher sought is found.
elements.mainPoint: **All the treasures of wisdom** are hidden in Christ.

elements.passageText: 11“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. 12The hired hand, who is not a shepherd and does not own sheep, sees the wolf coming and abandons the sheep and runs away. So the wolf attacks the sheep and scatters them. 13Because he is a hired hand and is not concerned about the sheep, he runs away. 14“I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me— 15just as the Father knows me and I know the Father—and I lay down my life for the sheep. 16I have other sheep that do not come from this sheepfold. I must bring them too, and they will listen to my voice, so that there will be one flock and one shepherd. 17This is why the Father loves me —because I lay down my life, so that I may take it back again. 18No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down of my own free will. I have the authority to lay it down, and I have the authority to take it back again. This commandment I received from my Father.”

elements.question: In John 10:11–18, what does the good shepherd do for his sheep, and how is he contrasted with the hired hand?
elements.questionHint: Look for what he lays down and what the hired hand does when the wolf comes.
elements.sampleAnswer: The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep, and knows his own, as the Father knows him. The hired hand, who does not own the sheep, runs away when the wolf comes. Jesus says that he has other sheep too, so that there will be one flock and one shepherd, and that he lays down his life of his own free will and has authority to take it back again.
elements.mainPoint: Jesus is **the good shepherd who lays down his life** for the sheep.

elements.passageText: 9So then whether we are alive or away, we make it our ambition to please him. 10For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may be paid back according to what he has done while in the body, whether good or evil. 11Therefore, because we know the fear of the Lord, we try to persuade people, but we are well known to God, and I hope we are well known to your consciences too. 12We are not trying to commend ourselves to you again, but are giving you an opportunity to be proud of us, so that you may be able to answer those who take pride in outward appearance and not in what is in the heart. 13For if we are out of our minds, it is for God; if we are of sound mind, it is for you. 14For the love of Christ controls us, since we have concluded this, that Christ died for all; therefore all have died. 15And he died for all so that those who live should no longer live for themselves but for him who died for them and was raised.

elements.question: In 2 Corinthians 5:10 Paul says we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ. In verses 14–15, what controls Paul and those with him, and why? How does this affect the way God’s judgment in Ecclesiastes 12:14 is received?
elements.questionHint: Read verse 10 and verses 14–15 together.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says that the love of Christ controls him and those with him, since Christ died for all, and he died so that those who live should no longer live for themselves but for him who died for them and was raised. The judgment that every deed will face is real, as in Ecclesiastes. But it is faced by people for whom Christ has died and been raised, so that fear of God and the love of Christ belong together.
elements.mainPoint: **The love of Christ** controls us: he died and was raised for us, so we live for him and face judgment as those he redeemed.

elements.text: Reflect

elements.question: Do you tend to hold back from enjoying life, or to forget God in the enjoying? What would ‘rejoice’ and ‘remember your Creator’ together look like for you?
The Teacher pictures old age and death very frankly. How comfortable are you thinking about your own, and what helps you face it?
Looking back over all eight sessions, what has Ecclesiastes changed or confirmed for you? What will you take away?

elements.text: That is the end of the study, but not of the book. If you would like to read the parts we skipped, they are 1:12–18, 4:13–16, 5:8–9, chapters 6 to 8, and 9:13–11:6. The whole book can be read in under an hour, and it reads very differently once you know its shape.

blocks.title: Eight sessions, eight passages
blocks.body: Ecclesiastes is a short book, but it is not easy. This study reads eight representative passages. At the start of most sessions you will find a short summary of the part of the book we skipped, and an If you have time box suggesting what to read to catch up.

blocks.title: Looking to Christ
blocks.body: Every session has a short section on how the passage connects with Christ and the New Testament. Read the New Testament passage on its own terms first, then ask how it relates to what the Teacher says.

blocks.title: Reading the key word
blocks.body: The book’s key word, which the NET renders ‘futile’, appears in other translations as ‘vanity’, ‘meaningless’, ‘emptiness’ or ‘vapour’. The Hebrew word means something like a breath. Do not be thrown if your own Bible words it differently.

blocks.title: A quick map
blocks.body:
Ecclesiastes has twelve chapters. A narrator introduces the Teacher at the start (1:1–2), the Teacher then speaks for himself, and a narrator speaks again at the end (12:8–14). In between, the Teacher keeps returning to one question: what lasting benefit do people get from their work and their days? The eight sessions visit the book like this:

  • 1:1–11 The question is posed (session 1).
  • 1:12–2:26 Wisdom, pleasure and work are tested (session 2; 1:12–18 is summarised).
  • 3:1–22 Time, God’s work and death (session 3).
  • 4:1–5:7 Oppression, toil, companionship and worship (sessions 4 and 5; 4:13–16 is summarised).
  • 5:8–8:17 Money, wisdom and justice (session 6 reads 5:10–20; the rest is summarised before sessions 6 and 7).
  • 9:1–12 Death and the days we have (session 7).
  • 9:13–11:6 Wisdom, folly and acting when the future is hidden (summarised before session 8).
  • 11:7–12:14 Youth, old age and the closing voice (session 8).

blocks.title: Three things to listen for
blocks.body: Listen for the word ‘futile’, for the phrase ‘on earth’ (many translations say ‘under the sun’), which draws attention to what can be seen in this life, and for the repeated advice to enjoy God’s gifts. That advice comes back in sessions 2, 3, 6 and 7.

blocks.title: Before you meet
blocks.body: If you can, read the passage and write answers to the questions beforehand. Reading the ‘What we skipped’ summary and, if there is time, the catch-up passage will help.

blocks.title: When you meet
blocks.body: A session takes about 60 to 75 minutes. Start with the opening question, read the passage aloud, work through the passage questions, then spend time on Looking to Christ. Keep the reflection questions for the end, and share only as much as you wish.

blocks.title: For leaders
blocks.body: If you are leading, there are Leaders’ Notes for every session. Switch them on under Settings → App → Optional Pages → Leaders’ Notes (this needs Intermediate interface mode).

blocks.title: Pace yourself
blocks.body: One session a week works well. Write an answer to every question before you look at the sample answer; the Check button will tell you how your answer compares.

blocks.title: Reading the whole book
blocks.body: Ecclesiastes can be read in under an hour. If you want to see how the sessions fit together, read the whole book once before you start, or after you finish.

leadersNotesData.subtitle: Notes for group leaders
intro: These notes are for anyone leading a group. Each session has an aim, some advice on leading the questions, things to watch for, and a note on the Looking to Christ section.

A session of about 70 minutes might run like this: opening question (5 minutes), reading the passage aloud and the passage questions (30), Looking to Christ (15), reflection questions (15), and a closing prayer (5). If time is short, shorten the passage questions and keep the reflection.
Nothing in these notes is secret, but they are written for leaders. Do not feel you must have every answer: the sample answers and hints in the study will carry most of the load.

aim.body: To meet the Teacher’s central question, what lasting benefit human effort brings, and to notice that the book is honest rather than cynical. The group should leave knowing how the study works and feeling free to be honest.

lead.body:
The question about the two voices (verses 1–2) will be new to most groups. Let people notice the third person for themselves, and do not push a theory about who the second voice is.

The question about the Teacher’s real complaint is the hinge of the session. Steer the group towards ‘no lasting gain’ rather than ‘life is pointless’.

The reflection questions are personal. Invite sharing, and do not require it.

watch.body:
Some people hear ‘everything is futile’ as the Bible endorsing despair, and some are surprised that such a book is in the Bible. Reassure them that we are letting the Teacher speak and that we shall read to the end.

If someone asks who wrote it: the book names ‘the Teacher’, son of David, king in Jerusalem. Scholars differ on how directly that points to Solomon, and the study does not depend on the answer.

christ.body: Romans 8 is the clearest New Testament echo of the Teacher’s word. Let the group notice that Paul agrees that creation is under futility, and then says who put it there and in hope of what. The Teacher’s observation is true as far as it goes; Paul says where it goes next.

aim.body: To watch the Teacher test pleasure, achievement and wisdom, and to hear his first positive conclusion: enjoyment is a gift from God, not a prize to be earned.

lead.body:
The question about joy in verse 10 and ‘profitless’ in verse 11 is the key. Expect someone to say the Teacher contradicts himself; help the group see that he separates present enjoyment from lasting gain.

The question on verse 26 is hard. Do not force an answer; ask only what each group is given.

There are two Looking to Christ passages this week, so keep an eye on the clock.

watch.body:
Verse 26 can be heard as saying that the rich are wicked, or the poor righteous. The verse says neither.

The passage about leaving the fruit of your work to someone else (2:18–23) can be painful for people thinking about family, a business or an estate. Leave space.

christ.body: With Luke 12, let the group see the overlap with chapter 2: death, who gets it, and eating and drinking. With 1 Corinthians 1, the Teacher says the wise man dies like the fool, and Paul says Christ is the wisdom of God. Do not claim that the Teacher was thinking of Christ; ask how Christ answers the problem the Teacher states.

aim.body: To read the famous poem in its setting: God appoints the times, we cannot see the whole of what he is doing, and the Teacher is left with open questions about justice and death.

lead.body:
Sorting the pairs of the poem is a good warm-up; let people argue about ‘a time to hate’. For verse 11, point to the translation note and do not spend long on the ‘eternity’ debate.

The Teacher’s ‘who really knows?’ in verse 21 is a real question. Do not answer it too quickly; the Looking to Christ section does that.

watch.body:
Verses 18–21 are sometimes read as saying that humans are ‘just animals’. Point to what verse 19 actually says (the same death, the same breath) and that the passage ends with a question, not a doctrine.

Memories of funerals may surface when the group reads the poem.

christ.body: Galatians 4 answers the theme of times: God had an appropriate time, and it centred on his Son. Acts 17 answers the Teacher’s hope of judgment and his question about death: God has set a day and has given proof by raising a man from the dead.

aim.body: To face oppression, envy and loneliness honestly, and to see the value of companionship.

lead.body:
Let the group feel the weight of 4:1–3 before moving on. The Teacher is reporting how bleak it looks, not recommending that people should not be born.

The questions about the lonely man and about the answer in verses 9–12 work as a pair. The last passage question is a good place to bring in real situations from the group.

watch.body:
People in the group may be oppressed, isolated or bereaved, or may work in situations of rivalry. Do not use verses 9–12 as a quick fix for loneliness, and do not press anyone to disclose.

Avoid reading the three-stranded cord as the Trinity, or as ‘you, me and God’. The verse is a proverb about strength in numbers.

christ.body: In Luke 4 Jesus applies Isaiah’s words to himself with the word ‘today’. In Galatians 6 the church is called to carry one another’s burdens. The Teacher saw no one comforting the oppressed; the New Testament calls the church to be the ‘two’.

aim.body: To learn from the Teacher how to approach God: listen first, speak little, and keep what you promise.

lead.body:
Take care with ‘let your words be few’. It would be wrong to read it as a ban on long prayer. Ask what the passage is guarding against: rash vows and hasty speech.

On vows, invite the group to name modern equivalents: promises made in prayer, membership or ministry commitments, and marriage vows.

watch.body:
Someone may feel shame about a promise to God that they have not kept. The passage is blunt, so bring in the mercy and grace of Hebrews 4:16 early.

Some may hear the passage as ‘God does not want to hear from me’. It says the opposite: he is worth listening to.

christ.body: Hebrews 4 keeps both sides: it is still a throne, and the high priest sympathises with our weakness. Encourage the group to hold care and confidence together, rather than choosing one.

aim.body: To see how the love of money fails to satisfy, and how wealth can be received as a gift from God.

lead.body: The question about the labourer’s sleep usually produces good discussion. In the last two passage questions, keep the contrast on attitudes, not amounts of money.

watch.body:
Group members may be anxious about money, or well off. Avoid judging either.

Verses 18–20 do not support a prosperity message. They say enjoyment is a gift from God, and chapter 6 (which we skipped) shows that the gift can be withheld even from the rich.

christ.body: Paul in 1 Timothy 6 says what the Teacher says about the gift of God, and adds generosity and a treasure for the future. Let the group see how contentment and generosity go together.

aim.body: To face death and unpredictability, to receive the Teacher’s call to enjoy life wholeheartedly now, and to see how the resurrection of Christ changes the picture.

lead.body:
The last passage question is the central one: how does the command to enjoy follow from death and chance? Allow space; some will find the passage too grim, and others too comforting.

Verses 5–6 speak of the dead having no share in what happens on earth. Do not use them to build a doctrine of what happens to people after death.

watch.body:
Someone in the group may have lost a loved one recently. Offer to pause, or to skip the opening question.

The skipped chapters 6–8 contain some of the hardest verses in the book. Do not feel that the group must read them first.

christ.body: Let the group hold two verses side by side: ‘no work in the grave’ (Ecclesiastes 9:10) and ‘your labour is not in vain’ (1 Corinthians 15:58). The resurrection does not cancel the Teacher’s call to enjoy life; it gives it deeper ground.

aim.body: To finish the book: joy together with remembering the Creator, the pictures of old age, the voice that frames the Teacher, and the final conclusion. Leave time to look back over the whole study.

lead.body:
For the question about who is speaking, help the group see the ‘I’ of 1:12 against the third person of 12:8–11. Do not insist on a theory of how the book was edited. What matters is that the book closes with a voice that sums up and gives the conclusion.

The conclusion about fearing God is not a contrast with the Teacher’s joy; it is the ground of it. Keep at least 15 minutes for the last reflection question.

watch.body:
The pictures in 12:1–7 are poetic, and people disagree about them. Do not spend long identifying each one.

The judgment in 11:9 and 12:14 can be heard as a threat. The Christ section shows how judgment is faced by those for whom Christ died.

Readers differ about ‘one shepherd’ in 12:11. Do not settle it.

christ.body: The epilogue calls the Teacher wise. The New Testament presents Christ as the true wise man, in whom the treasures of wisdom are hidden (Colossians 2:3; 1 Corinthians 1:30). Let the group see how the wise man of the book points to him, though the book does not say so itself.
